opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that people often treat distillation as one recipe, when really it's a design space, and where you land in it should depend on what you actually want the student to be good at.

So I usually start by asking: what does the student need to do at deployment time? If it's going to be generating long sequences on its own, like reasoning traces or code, then the big issue is that the student will visit states the teacher never showed it. Standard distillation, where you train on teacher-generated outputs or match the teacher's token distributions on a fixed dataset, has a train–test mismatch. During training the student only ever sees prefixes the teacher produced, but at inference it's conditioning on its own mistakes, and errors compound.

That's a lot of what motivated our work on on-policy distillation, sometimes called generalized knowledge distillation. The idea is simple: let the student generate its own samples, then ask the teacher for feedback on those samples, basically token-level probabilities on the student's own trajectories. Now the student learns how to recover from the states it actually ends up in. It's very close in spirit to imitation learning ideas like DAgger, just applied to language models.

The second knob is the divergence you optimize. Forward KL makes the student cover all of the teacher's modes, which can be bad when the student is much smaller and doesn't have capacity, because it ends up spreading probability mass over junk. Reverse KL is more mode-seeking, so the student commits to a few high-quality behaviors. Depending on whether you care about diversity or about getting the top answer right, you'd choose differently, and there are interpolations like Jensen–Shannon in between.

Third, there's the data mixture: how much fixed teacher data versus on-policy student data. Teacher data is cheaper since you can generate it offline once, and it's a decent starting point. On-policy data costs more because you need the teacher in the loop, but it's where a lot of the gains come from, especially on harder reasoning tasks.

Finally, distillation fits naturally with RL. If you already have a reward signal, on-policy distillation is just another form of dense feedback, and the teacher gives you per-token signal instead of one sparse reward at the end. In practice that can make it much more sample-efficient than pure RL for getting a small model up to speed. You can even combine the two, with the teacher shaping the policy and the reward keeping it grounded in what you actually care about.

So the short version: work backward from the student's deployment behavior, make sure it trains on the distribution it'll actually face, and pick your divergence based on capacity and whether you want diversity or precision.

r001.rationale: The response discusses designing distillation around deployment behavior, but does not say teacher selection should depend on whether the student will serve directly or undergo further post-training.

r002.rationale: It says distillation can be combined with RL, but does not propose that RL after extensive distillation may yield additional improvements.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that further training may be unnecessary when distillation brings the student sufficiently close to the teacher on relevant tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that distillation is often framed as a compression problem, like you have a big model and you want a smaller model that behaves the same way, and I actually think that framing is a bit limiting. The way I like to think about it is, you start from the end. What is the student actually going to be doing? What's the deployment context, what's the latency budget, what's the distribution of inputs it's going to see? Because those answers change almost every design decision upstream.

So concretely, the first question is what data you're distilling on. The classic approach is you take some fixed dataset, you run the teacher on it, you get labels or logits, and you train the student to match. And that works, but it has this mismatch problem. The student at inference time is generating its own sequences, and those sequences look different from what the teacher wrote. So the student has only ever seen the teacher's trajectories, and when it drifts a little, it's in territory it was never trained on. That's a lot of what we were trying to address with on-policy distillation, where you let the student sample, and then you have the teacher provide the signal on the student's own outputs. You're training on the distribution the student will actually live in.

The second thing is what signal you're matching. If you only care about final correctness, say math or code where you can verify the answer, then maybe you don't need the teacher's full distribution at all, you just need to know whether the student got it right, and that starts to look more like RL. But if you care about things like calibration, or style, or behavior on open-ended tasks, then matching the teacher's distribution, the token-level or sequence-level KL, carries a lot more information per sample than a scalar reward does. So a lot of my thinking is about where on that spectrum you want to be. Dense distribution-matching signal is very sample efficient, but it also means you inherit the teacher's mistakes. Sparse outcome signal lets the student potentially exceed the teacher on verifiable tasks, but it's noisier and slower.

And then the third piece, which people underrate, is that the teacher doesn't have to be a single fixed model. It can be the same model with more test-time compute, more samples, a verifier filtering the outputs. So you're really distilling a system, not a model. Once you see it that way, the pipeline question becomes, what's the most expensive thing I'm willing to run offline, and what's the cheap thing I need at inference, and how do I move capability from one to the other with the least loss on the tasks I actually care about. I'd rather have a student that's great on the narrow distribution it's going to serve than one that's a uniformly slightly worse copy of the teacher.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deployment context and teacher-system design, but does not say teacher selection should depend on whether the student will serve directly or undergo further post-training.

r002.rationale: It compares distribution matching with RL and says sparse outcome signals may let a student exceed its teacher, but does not propose applying RL after extensive distillation.

r003.rationale: It favors a student that performs well on its target tasks, but does not state that further training may be unnecessary when the student is sufficiently close to the teacher.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to work backward from what you need the student to do. Are you trying to preserve the teacher’s capabilities broadly, or do you want a smaller model that’s really good at a particular task? And what are your constraints on latency and inference cost? Those decisions should drive the pipeline.

Then there’s the question of what data the student learns from. You can generate high-quality answers from a teacher, but if those answers are on inputs that don’t resemble what the student will encounter, you may be optimizing the wrong thing. So I’d start with an evaluation that reflects the intended use, and use that to guide the training distribution.

Another important distinction is whether the student is learning only from teacher-generated responses or also from its own attempts. When the student generates something, you get to see where it actually struggles. Teacher feedback on those attempts can be more targeted than simply giving it more demonstrations.

So I’d treat distillation as an iterative process: define the behavior you want, train a student, examine the failures, and adjust the data and supervision. The goal is to make the student useful under your constraints, and that doesn’t necessarily require copying every aspect of the teacher.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing the student’s goals and constraints, but does not say teacher selection depends on whether the student will serve directly or receive further post-training.

r002.rationale: It describes iterative training and targeted teacher feedback, but does not propose RL after extensive distillation as a source of additional improvement.

r003.rationale: It says the student need not copy every aspect of the teacher, but does not state that further training may be unnecessary when the student is sufficiently close on the tasks of interest.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you start with what you want the student to be good at, and then work backward. Is it a general-purpose assistant, or is it solving a fairly narrow set of tasks? What are your constraints on latency and inference cost? Those decisions should shape the data you collect and what you ask the teacher to produce.

For example, if you care about reasoning, you might want the teacher to generate intermediate reasoning rather than just final answers. But you also need to ask whether those examples are learnable by the student. A response that’s excellent for a very large model isn’t necessarily the best training signal for a much smaller one.

So I’d treat it as an iterative loop: train a student, evaluate it on the behavior you actually care about, look at where it fails, and use the teacher to generate or improve data for those gaps. The objective isn’t just to imitate the teacher. It’s to get the best student you can under the constraints you have.

r001.rationale: The response says teacher outputs should reflect the student’s goals and constraints, but does not distinguish distillation for the final serving model from preparation for further post-training.

r002.rationale: It describes an iterative train, evaluate, and improve-data loop, but does not propose using RL after extensive distillation.

r003.rationale: It recommends evaluating the student on desired behaviors, but does not say further training may be unnecessary once distillation brings it sufficiently close to the teacher.
